readerTitle: Your rent is going up 15%. Here's what to do before you reply.
caseNote: 가상 사례 (애견 미용실 임대 갱신, 소형 물류 창고 임대 갱신) · 모든 수치는 설명용
insight: 임대료 협상은 집주인에게 답장을 쓸 때가 아니라 이사 비용을 계산하고 집주인이 왜 올리는지 물을 때 시작된다.
misconception: 임대료 인상 통보는 받아들이거나 반으로 깎는 것 말고는 방법이 없다. 더 싼 곳이 있다고 말하면 협상력이 생긴다.

sources.text: Fisher, R. & Ury, W. (1981). Getting to Yes. (BATNA, 입장과 이해관계의 구분)

factChecks.note: 임대차 계약의 법적 조건(갱신권, 인상 상한 등)은 나라와 지역마다 다릅니다. 카드 7에서 현지 확인을 권하는 수준으로만 다루고 법률 조언은 하지 않았습니다.

cards.title: Your rent is going up 15%. Here's what to do before you reply.
body: Maya runs a dog grooming salon. Her five-year lease ends in three months. Today a letter arrives: the new rent will be $3,450 a month, up from $3,000.
Most owners do one of two things. They sign, or they write back asking for less. Both skip the two steps that decide how this ends.

image.label: Lease renewal letter on a grooming salon counter
image.brief: 3D 클레이 스타일. 애견 미용실 카운터 위에 놓인 편지 한 장, "Rent: $3,000 → $3,450" 문구가 크게 보임. 뒤편에 미용 테이블과 강아지 한 마리. 실제 브랜드나 로고는 쓰지 않음.

cards.title: What should Maya do first?
body: She has three months before the lease ends. The landlord wants an answer within a month.

options.text: Write back with a counteroffer of $3,100
options.feedback: A clear first number can help. But she'd be picking it blind, without knowing what staying is actually worth to her.

options.text: Price out a real move to another space before replying
options.feedback: This is her **best alternative** (BATNA): what she'd do if no deal happens. Knowing it tells her which offers beat walking away.

options.text: Sign quickly to stay on good terms
options.feedback: She keeps the goodwill and avoids the hassle. She may also pay $27,000 more over five years than she needed to.

cards.title: What moving would really cost over five years.
body: A space two streets away rents for $2,900. Cheaper, until you add the move. Spread over 60 months, moving works out to about **$3,350 a month**. Staying at $3,450 costs $6,000 more. Her alternative is real, but only slightly better.
cards.callout: Anything above about $3,350 a month is worse than moving.

cards.title: The landlord has an alternative too.
body: If Maya leaves, the landlord's **best alternative** is finding a new tenant. That means an empty unit, agent fees and possibly a new fit-out for someone else.
Even two empty months would cost $6,900 in lost rent at the new price. So the landlord's alternative is weaker than the letter suggests.
Maya now knows both sides' fallback. Neither wants to walk away. That's room to talk.

cards.title: Ask why the rent is going up.
body: $3,450 is the landlord's **position**: what they asked for. The reasons behind it are their **interests**.
Maya asks. The landlord's insurance and property taxes rose, and they want steady income they can count on. Maya's interest is different: cash is tight this year, but business is growing.
Now a new deal appears. A seven-year lease starting at $3,150, rising 3% a year. The landlord gets a long, reliable tenant. Maya gets breathing room now.

image.label: Two sides of a table, positions on top, interests underneath
image.brief: 빙산 두 개가 테이블 양쪽에 있는 인포그래픽. 수면 위에는 "$3,450"과 "$3,000", 수면 아래에는 "Steady income", "Rising costs"(집주인), "Cash this year", "Room to grow"(마야). 두 빙산 아래쪽이 연결됨.

cards.softwareNote: The same moves work when a software vendor raises your subscription at renewal. Price the switch, including migration and retraining, then ask what the vendor wants. Often it's a longer commitment, not a higher price.

cards.title: "That's the market rate."
body: At the meeting, the landlord repeats: the rent is $3,450, and that's the market. What should Maya say?

options.text: "The place down the street is $2,900. I'll pay $2,900."
options.feedback: It uses her alternative as a threat and overstates it. Moving really costs her about $3,350 a month, and the landlord may call the bluff.

options.text: "I want to stay. What's behind the increase?"
options.feedback: It moves the talk from **positions** to **interests**. Once she hears about costs and steady income, she can offer a longer lease instead of a higher price.

options.text: "Can we meet in the middle at $3,225?"
options.feedback: Fast and fair-sounding, and better than her alternative. But splitting the difference trades only on price and misses deals both sides prefer.

cards.title: An alternative only helps if it's real.
body: Don't claim a cheaper space you wouldn't actually take. If the landlord says "go ahead," you lose credibility and possibly the unit.
Moving costs are easy to underestimate. Regular customers who know your street, permits, new signage: count them before you rely on leaving.
Lease rules also differ by country and city. Check your local terms, such as renewal rights or notice periods, before you negotiate.

cards.title: Now it's a warehouse.
body: Tom runs a small warehouse that stores and ships orders for local online shops. His landlord wants 10% more rent at renewal. Moving his racking would cost about $40,000, and the nearest suitable unit is 30 km away.

options.text: Tell the landlord he's found a cheaper unit nearby
options.feedback: A bluffed alternative is fragile. His real **BATNA** is expensive, and a landlord who knows the area may see that.

options.text: Price the move, then ask what the landlord needs most
options.feedback: He learns how much the 10% is really worth fighting over (**BATNA**), then looks for trades like a longer lease or a new loading door (**interests**).

options.text: Accept, since moving the racking costs too much
options.feedback: Staying may well be right given his weak alternative. But accepting without asking why leaves possible trades on the table.

cards.title: Price your exit, then ask why.
body: This lesson used two ideas. **Your best alternative** told Maya what staying was worth. **Interests vs positions** turned one number into a better deal for both sides.
**Try it today:** take your biggest recurring contract, such as rent, a lease or a key subscription. Write down what leaving would really cost, then one reason the other side might want to keep you.
